extracted.intended_audience: EPA rulewriters, state permitting authorities, EGU owners/operators, industry stakeholders, environmental regulators, and commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria used by the EPA to determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for coal-fired steam electric generating units, including cost-reasonableness, environmental/health impacts, energy impacts, permitting, and comparisons to prior rulemakings and technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost metrics for assessing cost reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA developed two metrics for assessing the cost reasonableness of controls: the increase in cost of electricity due to controls, measured in $/MWh, and the control costs of removing a ton of pollutant, measured in $/ton CO2e. The costs presented are in 2019 dollars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The EPA uses these metrics as useful indicators (not bright-line standards). Example benchmarks referenced include $18.50/MWh and $98/ton CO2e; controls generally consistent with those levels should be considered reasonable. These metrics are used alongside a broader range of cost information to conclude whether costs of identified BSERs are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to costs of prior required controls (FGD, SCR) as benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the costs of GHG control measures to the costs of controls EPA has previously required in the power sector (e.g., flue gas desulfurization (FGD) for SO2; selective catalytic reduction (SCR) for NOX).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because EPA previously required these controls and the industry installed them, their historical per-MWh costs (e.g., wet FGD retrofits annualized costs of $14.80–$18.50/MWh for 700–300 MW units; SCR retrofit costs of $10.60–$11.80/MWh) provide a benchmark for reasonableness of new control costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to GHG control costs in other industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare per-ton cost-effectiveness to other industries' GHG control costs (e.g., oil and gas methane reductions previously estimated at $2,447/ton converted to $98/ton CO2e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using cross-industry precedents helps determine whether a $/ton level is reasonable; EPA notes prior regulatory decisions in other industries that required controls at comparable $/ton levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of updated CCS costs and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Re-evaluate CCS cost reasonableness in light of updated NETL cost estimates (2015 vs 2022) and changes to IRC section 45Q tax credit (increase from $50 to $85/metric ton, with other adjustments and monetization options).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites NETL: 2015 incremental levelized CCS cost $74/MWh (2022$) vs 2022 estimate $44/MWh (2022$). The combination of lower costs and increased 45Q value materially improves the cost reasonableness of CCS for BSER determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-air quality health and environmental impacts (including water use, transport, sequestration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider non-GHG emissions impacts, water use impacts, transport and sequestration of captured CO2, and energy requirements resulting from CCS when evaluating BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where potential localized adverse consequences exist, the EPA assesses whether protections are in place to mitigate those risks (e.g., UIC, GHGRP, PHMSA). EPA discusses energy requirements first because they are closely related to non-air quality impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy requirements and energy penalty assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess parasitic/auxiliary energy demand and resulting net power output/efficiency reductions for units applying CCS (example: a ~474 MW-net unit without CCS to ~425 MW-net with CCS; ~23% net efficiency reduction for 90% amine-based capture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Auxiliary heat/power sources are part of the designated facility and subject to standards; any CO2 emissions from auxiliary equipment must be captured or will affect facility emission rate. EPA considers the energy penalty relatively minor compared to GHG reduction benefits and not unreasonable for BSER purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation and permitting of non-GHG co-pollutant impacts (SO2, PM)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that amine-based CO2 capture can increase emissions of SO2 and PM; mitigation typically requires flue gas conditioning and additional controls (e.g., FGD scrubber, polishing column, WESP, upgraded PM controls).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA assumes CCS retrofits will require installation of SCR and/or FGD where not already present; NSR permitting (major or minor) provides regulatory backstops (LAER, BACT, offsets) to review and mitigate remaining increases. Costs for these controls are included in compliance cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: NOX impacts, solvent degradation, and nitrosamine formation
rubrics_metrics.description: NOX emissions can cause solvent degradation and nitrosamine formation; requisite NOX limits vary and may require existing combustion controls or installation of SCR to protect capture process function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities may apply major NSR (triggering SCR) or use state plan enforceable limits to avoid major NSR triggers; where increases are lesser, minor NSR provisions determine controls. EPA plans to update NSR permitting guidance, specifically BACT determinations for GHGs and co-pollutant increases from CCS.

rubrics_metrics.name: HAPs and VOC emissions from solvent degradation and controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Solvent degradation can produce HAPs and VOCs (e.g., nitrosamines, formaldehyde, acetaldehyde); controls such as multistage water/acid wash and demisters are effective for amines and many degradation products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A separate controls system may be needed for aldehydes; some control technologies (electrochemical, UV) are under development and may have limited efficacy. If a carbon capture system is a major source of listed HAPs, applicability of CAA section 112(g) and a case-by-case MACT analysis should be evaluated. Measurement of nitrosamines may be challenging at very low concentrations (<1 ppb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Air toxics assessment and permit-based emission limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Air permit applications should include potential-to-emit (PTE) and air toxics assessments (example: Project Tundra PTE values and resulting risk/hazard index comparisons to ND-DEQ thresholds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits may establish limits for specific HAPs (formaldehyde, acetaldehyde) based on testing after initial operation. Results will depend on flue gas conditions, solvent choice, source size, process design, stack height, local ambient conditions, and exposed population location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stationary source aggregation criteria for permitting (EGU vs CO2 capture plant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an EGU and a CO2 capture plant are a single stationary source under NSR by applying criteria: (1) same industrial grouping (SIC), (2) contiguous/adjacent properties, (3) common control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA expects most collocated capture plants will meet aggregation criteria because of functional interdependence (steam, electricity, flue gas), shared location/adjacency, contractual relationships, and operational interactions; therefore permitting as separate sources is generally not expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water use and cooling system design considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate increased water consumption due to solvent makeup and cooling demand (gross increases up to ~36%) and cooling system design choices (dedicated systems, reliance on condensed flue gas, dry/hybrid cooling for limited-water regions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (e.g., condensate-only systems) can avoid increased external water consumption. EPA considers water use requirements manageable and not a categorical barrier to CCS installation.

rubrics_metrics.name: CO2 capture plant siting and land-use assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the physical footprint and land requirements of capture systems; assess land availability adjacent to units (example analysis showed high adjacent availability for most >300 MW units).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reviewed data/maps and concluded siting/land-use needs are not unreasonable for coal-fired plants generally; longer duct runs might be required in some cases but do not preclude CCS installation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transport and geologic sequestration protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess safety and environmental protections for CO2 transport and sequestration, including PHMSA oversight of pipelines and UIC Class VI/II regulations, plus GHGRP reporting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PHMSA incident history and rulemaking, together with UIC and GHGRP (subparts RR and VV), provide an effective regulatory framework that EPA considered in determining CCS as BSER for long-term steam EGUs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impacts on power sector structure and reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate nationwide and long-term impacts of designating CCS as BSER on power sector structure and grid reliability, including projected adoption and timelines (e.g., projected GW applying CCS by 2035) and planning needs for installation downtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concluded designation would have limited and non-adverse long-term impacts on structure or reliability; planning horizon (compliance deadline Jan 1, 2032) allows adequate resource planning. Reliability impacts are discussed further in the preamble (section XII.F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of CO2 emission reductions achievable with CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the magnitude of emission rate reductions (e.g., CCS can reduce CO2 mass by 90% or more; 90% capture yields ~88.4% lb/MWh-gross reduction and ~87.1% lb/MWh-net reduction per NETL Retrofit report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because coal-fired plants are high absolute emitters, high-percentage capture yields very large absolute reductions. Increased utilization incentivized by 45Q does not negate substantial emission rate reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of technology development as part of BSER consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether designating a technology as BSER will meaningfully advance deployment and improvement of that technology (EPA modeling indicated increased CCS installations and generation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designation can support broader CCS advances across the power sector and potentially other industries; EPA used IPM modeling to quantify likely installations and generation increases attributable to the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with prior NSPS determinations and approach to revising new-source standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare current BSER decisions to prior New Source Performance Standards (e.g., 2015 NSPS for new coal-fired EGUs adopted CCS with 16–23% capture based on costs at that time) and evaluate whether to revise existing new-source standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes cost declines since 2015 would change capture percentage if new-source standards were revisited, but declines in new coal construction plans mean EPA does not currently propose revising the 2015 NSPS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, reporting, and transfer requirements under GHGRP (40 CFR part 98)
rubrics_metrics.description: Require EGUs that capture CO2 to report under the GHGRP (40 CFR part 98), including subpart PP and relevant subparts (RR, VV) to quantify storage and identify/address leakage. If injection occurs offsite, EGUs must transfer captured CO2 to a facility that reports under subpart RR or VV or to a facility with an innovative technology waiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existing GHGRP mechanisms (subpart RR for Class VI wells; subpart VV for enhanced recovery when ISO 27916 used; MRV plan opt-in for Class II UIC wells) provide monitoring and reporting to ensure sequestration accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why partial-capture CCS is not BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Partial capture CCS was not determined to be BSER because emission reductions are lower and costs would generally be higher; 90% capture leverages economies of scale and better aligns with 45Q tax credit incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower capture rates receive fewer returns from 45Q (tied to amount sequestered) and may result in higher cost per ton; EPA finds 90% capture best balances BSER factors for long-term units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why natural gas co-firing not selected as BSER for long-term units
rubrics_metrics.description: Although 40% natural gas co-firing is determined to be BSER for medium-term subcategory, it was not selected for long-term units because variable costs are higher and total $/ton costs are generally higher than CCS for long-term units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA analyzed co-firing across all existing coal-fired units and found it adequately demonstrated for medium-term units, but for long-term units CCS provides more favorable overall cost-effectiveness and emissions outcomes; capital vs. variable cost tradeoffs discussed.
